messages.author: 83aa4ea66d984b54
messages.subject: Joint models of longitudinal and time-to-event data (with coarsened covariates)
parts: Hello everybody, I've just been looking at this new paper http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/sim.6242/abstract which proposes yet another slightly novel model for longitudinal + time-to-event data, and wondering why they bothered with extensive first-principles exposition of the likelihoods and then writing a one-off sampler in R. (Of course, the answer probably is a combination of the authors' mathematical expertise and the journal's fondness for algebraic exposition) Why not just write it in a graphical model style like Stan? They report getting 2000 iterations every 24 hours, and I find it hard to believe this is a sensible way to do it. Is there any reason why this sort of model can't be done in Stan?

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Joint models of longitudinal and time-to-event data (with coarsened covariates)
parts:
It's paywalled and statisticians are pretty much useless
as paper pirates. (I keep forgetting how to access papers
from Columbia remotely, but it's also a matter of principle for me; I
won't submit to or review for closed journals any more.)

It's not iterations, but time to convergence and then time
per effective sample after that that matters.

Stan's not just a graphical modeling language --- you can
write down any expression that's equal to the log posterior
up to an additive constant.

My general experience is that it's usually easy to fit
models that have continuous parameters in Stan. We've fit
all kinds of models that people have written complicated
software for. Most of those models could've been fit in
BUGS or JAGS, too, which would be easier than writing custom
code.

- Bob

messages.author: 83aa4ea66d984b54
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Joint models of longitudinal and time-to-event data (with coarsened covariates)
parts: Thanks Bob. Perhaps I've mixed up two points. First, Stan would be better than nuts n bolts in R, given points about continuous parameters etc. No point debating that in this forum. Second, I feel that journal readers are poorly served by pages of algebra and no straightforward BUGS/Stan code. With good checking, it should be ok to present a new model in this way. After all, I don't have to write down the likelihood and Newton-Raphson every time I publish a logistic regression.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Joint models of longitudinal and time-to-event data (with coarsened covariates)
parts:
I think this deserves a blog post! Here's a rough draft.

Robert grant writes,

> ... I feel that journal readers are poorly served by pages of algebra and no straightforward BUGS/Stan code. With good checking, it should be ok to present a new model in this way. After all, I don't have to write down the likelihood and Newton-Raphson every time I publish
> a logistic regression.

I (Bob) am always struck by this same issue. Here's what I
think is going on:

1. What goes in a paper is up to the author. If the author
struggled with a step or found it a bit tricky to think
about themselves, then the struggle goes into the paper. Even
if it might be obvious to someone with more experience in
a field. I was just reading a paper with a very detailed
exposition of EM for a latent logistic regression problem with
conditional probability derivations, etc. (JMLR paper on
crowdsourcing by Raykar et al., which by the way is an awesome
paper, even if it suffers from this flaw and number 3.)

2. What goes in a paper is up to editors. If the editors
don't understand something, they'll ask for details, even
if they should be obvious to the entire field. I find this
in applied papers in natural language processing, where
almost every paper that uses a notion like entropy (including
one I just wrote) redefines it from scratch. Every bit
of algebra gets worked out because the audience isn't used
to working equations for themselves. You have to insert p-values
even if you don't believe them. You have to justify Bayesian inference
by comparing it to some frequentist alternative. Etc., etc.
(Mitzi says whenever more than one academic gets togeter, the
topic eventually devolves to refereeing. Maybe it's just me.)

3. Authors tend to narratives over crisp expositions. They want
to tell you their story of how they got to the conclusions. (Even me,
hence the preface of the Stan manual.) One of the things that frustrates me
to no end in papers, particularly in statistics, is that the author tells you
a narrative of how they meandered to the model they finally use; in computer
science, they meander in the same way to models or algorithm
variants. What I want to see is a crisp statement of the model
with enough details that I can replicate it. Providing working code is the
easiest way to do that. It's why I liked Jennifer and Andrew's regression
book so much --- they gave you (mostly) runnable code.

I think what applied papers need to do is lay out their model crisply.
BUGS is a nice language for this if your model is easily expressed as a directed
acyclic graph. I think the variable declarations in Stan make it even clearer
what's going on, especially as models go beyond a few lines. The problem
with Stan, as Andrew and I were just discussing yesterday, is that you
have to lay out what is data and what is parameters (i.e., what you observe
and what you infer conditioned on those observations).

Mathematicians seem to be immune to problems (1) and (3). In fact, I
feel they often go too far, which is why this is such a Goldilocks issue.
What's an inscrutable step or bit of math to one person (contact manifolds
anyone?) is like a logistic regression to another person. You can't write
an intro to differentiable manifolds into every one of your papers.

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Joint models of longitudinal and time-to-event data (with coarsened covariates)
parts:
Contact manifolds are the worst!

I think that ultimately the issue is that people approach the unknown very differently.  The great scientists will understand they
don't have the time to understand something, find what bits they might be able to understand, but don't stop others from
exploring further.  Poor scientists will become defensive and prevent anyone from moving forward with methods/techniques
that they don't understand.

This frustrates publications, grants, algorithm adoption, and especially graduate advising.

One great thing about the Stan modeling language is that it defines a vocabulary in which people can describe their model
agnostic to the actual fitting methods.  That alone can go a long way to factoring the expertise needed to understand a paper.
